video_title: Recursive Language Models — Alex Zhang, MIT PhD
gist: MIT PhD Alex Zhang (transcribed 'Alex Jung') argues that harness design, not model architecture alone, is the under-exploited lever: Recursive Language Models (code-only REPL environments with recursive sub-agent calls and offloaded context) yield compositional, data-efficient generalization, while today's mainstream harnesses (Claude Code, Codex, Pi) are essentially identical loops. The conversation also covers OpenAI's ~$40M, 10,000-agent swarm result, Prime Agent, AI-automated GPU kernels and their verification limits, and why neolabs must bet on non-autoregressive paradigms. Note: the auto-transcript is a garbled machine translation, so several names are approximate.

themes.theme: RLMs and harness design as the real lever

insights.claim: A Recursive Language Model (RLM) is an environment design in which code is the only tool: the model runs in a REPL, can call itself programmatically as a sub-agent, and its full context lives in the program's memory or file system rather than in the prompt.
insights.speaker: Alex Zhang (guest, MIT PhD)
insights.so_what: RLM is a harness/inference pattern, not a new architecture; it can wrap any capable code-writing model.
insights.quote: RLM is, in essence, such design of an environment where the only tool there is a code.

insights.claim: Zhang argues that mainstream coding harnesses such as Claude Code, Codex and Pi are logically identical, essentially two model calls in a loop, so harness design remains a largely unexplored design space.
insights.speaker: Alex Zhang (guest, MIT PhD)
insights.so_what: Harness UX differences are a weak moat; differentiated harness logic is where untapped performance sits.
insights.quote: Two calls in cycle, and that's it.

insights.claim: The dominant training-environment class is 'trajectory as a prompt', in which the whole execution trajectory stays in the base model's context even when sub-agents are used. Because models are trained on this pattern, current frontier models are only 'normal' when plugged into RLM-style harnesses.
insights.speaker: Alex Zhang (guest, MIT PhD)
insights.so_what: Models post-trained natively on RLM-style environments could show a large jump. That favors whoever trains on new harness designs.

insights.claim: When RLMs are trained on search and aggregation tasks with very different prompts, the model learns the same root-level strategy for both, because sub-agents absorb the task-specific local work. Training on one task transfers to the other, and training on short tasks generalizes to much longer ones.
insights.speaker: Alex Zhang (guest, MIT PhD)
insights.so_what: Harness choice can multiply the data efficiency and generalization of post-training: more capability from fewer environments.

insights.claim: 'Locally in-distribution' framing: if a task is decomposed into a meta-program of sub-agent calls, every individual LM call can stay within the training distribution even when the overall task is out of distribution, which raises the odds that each step is correct.
insights.speaker: Alex Zhang (guest, MIT PhD)
insights.so_what: Explains why recursive decomposition beats single long-context calls on novel, long-horizon tasks.

insights.claim: Zhang believes there is a broad class of undiscovered harnesses with properties like RLM's, and that serious scaling experiments on post-training across different environment designs would yield significant gains.
insights.speaker: Alex Zhang (guest, MIT PhD)
insights.so_what: Open research gap: post-training scaling laws as a function of harness/environment design.

insights.claim: A further direction is training models to behave like an RLM implicitly inside the forward pass. Looped transformers are already analogous to applying a harness around a model.
insights.speaker: Alex Zhang (guest, MIT PhD)
insights.so_what: Harness logic could migrate into architecture, which would blur the line between model and scaffolding.

insights.claim: A recent environment-'tax' paper (attributed to Arena) found that most environment and harness choices are irrelevant and the main difference between them is cost. Zhang agrees that as models get smarter, plugging a strong model like Astra into an open-source harness works fine.
insights.speaker: Alex Zhang (guest, MIT PhD)
insights.so_what: For standard loop harnesses, cost, not capability, differentiates them; commoditization pressure on harness products.
insights.quote: Majority environmental elections are irrelevant because they are all the same.

insights.claim: Frontier labs almost certainly train only on their own environments, while open models such as Qwen work well with open-source harnesses and older Gemma-era models were known to be weak at this.
insights.speaker: Alex Zhang (guest, MIT PhD)
insights.so_what: Model-harness co-training creates lock-in: a lab's model performs best in its own harness.

insights.claim: In Zhang's long-running tests, Fable was the best model for RLM, which he attributes to training on dynamic worker processes (an acquired ability). Astra now also handles RLM tasks fairly well; these results are internal and unpublished.
insights.speaker: Alex Zhang (guest, MIT PhD)
insights.so_what: Recursive/orchestration skill is trainable and already differentiates frontier models.

insights.claim: Zhang predicts that what users perceive as a 'language model' will increasingly be a swarm, harness or complex system design that scales well, exposed through a simple chat or streaming interface.
insights.speaker: Alex Zhang (guest, MIT PhD)
insights.so_what: The product boundary shifts from weights to systems, so value accrues to the orchestration layer.

insights.claim: A frequent criticism of RLM was that it is 'just sub-agents' or 'not a language model'. Zhang counters that a language model only has to model language and need not be an autoregressive transformer decoder. He reads the dismissive reaction as a sign that people have not grasped the real goal.
insights.speaker: Alex Zhang (guest, MIT PhD)
insights.so_what: Simple ideas dismissed as trivial (like SWE-bench, ReAct) can define the next paradigm.

insights.claim: The real value of RLM is not the published idea but whether the system can be trained properly and architected around. Zhang says Prime and 'Select' are working on RLM training at scale, which MIT cannot afford.
insights.speaker: Alex Zhang (guest, MIT PhD)
insights.so_what: Startups training RLM-native models hold the moat, not the paper.

themes.theme: Prime Agent and RLM ecosystem adoption

insights.claim: Prime Agent is a harness built on top of the minimalist pi (pi mono) harness. IPython is its only tool, any other tool is loaded as a Python module or a bash script, and its context is offloaded to disk so the model can always return to the original context even after compression.
insights.speaker: Alex Zhang (guest, MIT PhD)
insights.so_what: A concrete open RLM-style harness to benchmark against Claude Code/Codex-style loops.

insights.claim: Prime Agent includes a 'continual harness' (developed by grad student Seth, originally for getting models to play games) that lets the agent modify parts of its own harness, such as its skills, its available sub-agents and its system prompt.
insights.speaker: Alex Zhang (guest, MIT PhD)
insights.so_what: Self-modifying harnesses are an early form of agent self-improvement without weight updates.

insights.claim: Prime Agent adds a code-based inter-agent communication system and persistent sub-agents that can outlive the original agent's run and accept new prompts. The host contrasts this with Codex's ephemeral sub-agents, which resist being used for long-running processes.
insights.speaker: Host
insights.so_what: Persistent, addressable sub-agents are a product gap in mainstream coding agents.

insights.claim: The core design rule behind these systems is to put everything in the file system and route everything through code, trusting the model to write whatever tools it needs.
insights.speaker: Host
insights.so_what: A cheap, general recipe any agent builder can adopt today.
insights.quote: The whole secret is that to take everything out file system, right?

insights.claim: Prime trains its own internal models for this harness and has spoken about it publicly since March. Zhang is not involved in that model training.
insights.speaker: Alex Zhang (guest, MIT PhD)
insights.so_what: Signals a neolab strategy of co-training model and harness rather than competing on base models.

insights.claim: Third-party adoption of RLM includes legal-AI company Harvey, which independently retrained RLM on legal document-review and retrieval work with very good results, an always-on 'constantly thinking' system from Andy Konwinski's institute that uses the RLM abstraction with token-cost controls, the DSPy-related Axe toolkit, and many ARC AGI 3 Kaggle entries that cite RLM-style tooling.
insights.speaker: Alex Zhang (guest, MIT PhD)
insights.so_what: RLM is getting real enterprise uptake in document-heavy verticals like legal.

themes.theme: Agent swarms and the economics of brute-force compute

insights.claim: OpenAI's swarm result (claimed 99.9% on ARC AGI 3 and a Navier-Stokes solution) used 10,000 agents for 88 hours and 130 billion output tokens. That is about $40 million at public prices, and more than double the tokens if inter-agent messages are counted.
insights.speaker: Host
insights.so_what: Frontier problem-solving now has a visible price tag (~$40M), so compute-for-results becomes a purchasable product.
insights.quote: 130 billion weekends tokens that estimated at approximately 40 million dollars at public prices.

insights.claim: Zhang thinks a model like GPT-6 Astra is technically smart enough to find such proofs given the right information. The hard part is obtaining that information, which likely came from a very long search across many swarm agents with a shared file-system context, possibly with researchers steering. The specific harness details mattered little.
insights.speaker: Alex Zhang (guest, MIT PhD)
insights.so_what: Value lies in how agents are combined and steered, not in the harness wrapper.

insights.claim: Zhang suspects roughly 95% of an agent swarm's work is useless token burning. He compares it to compaction versus RLM: RLM can solve harder tasks, but cheaper compaction is preferred in most cases.
insights.speaker: Alex Zhang (guest, MIT PhD)
insights.so_what: Swarm efficiency, measured as useful work per token, is the key objective and an optimization opportunity.

insights.claim: Effective agent swarms are not free emergent behavior from a smart model. OpenAI clearly trained its system to act as a swarm, and getting a swarm to converge on goals requires very careful harness design.
insights.speaker: Alex Zhang (guest, MIT PhD)
insights.so_what: Swarm capability is a trained, defensible asset, not a commodity wrapper.

insights.claim: The host speculates that OpenAI could package swarms as an API product (possibly branded 'Pro') where customers throw large budgets, even $40 million, at a problem and get a solution back.
insights.speaker: Host
insights.so_what: A potential new high-ticket revenue line: outcome-priced compute.

insights.claim: Cursor's multi-agent system architecture (as of February) converged on the org chart of a normal software team. The host argues that the coordinator's gather-all step is a bottleneck, analogous to synchronization in GPU programming.
insights.speaker: Host
insights.so_what: Hierarchical orchestration limits scaling; decentralized swarm designs may win.

insights.claim: A domain expert can steer a model away from spending a hundred billion or a trillion tokens on dead ends. Because there are too many problems to throw maximal compute at each one, efficiency remains critical.
insights.speaker: Alex Zhang (guest, MIT PhD)
insights.so_what: Human-in-the-loop expertise keeps a large cost advantage over brute-force agent search.

insights.claim: Zhang calls the release of 'dynamic workflows' a kind of failure: as he understands it, people often misuse it or it is simply too expensive, while the host likens it to handing over your bank account.
insights.speaker: Alex Zhang (guest, MIT PhD)
insights.so_what: Expensive multi-agent features face adoption risk unless cost per useful outcome falls.

insights.claim: Kimi's agent swarm looks interesting, but it is unclear whether it can solve anything new. Its pitch amounts to 'here is a swarm that does something', such as building spreadsheets.
insights.speaker: Alex Zhang (guest, MIT PhD)
insights.so_what: Swarm marketing outpaces demonstrated novel capability.

themes.theme: GPU kernels: AI automation, verification and saturation

insights.claim: GPU kernel programming resembles competitive programming: people use a surprisingly limited set of optimizations on a small set of kernels. That motivated GPU Mode's Popcorn leaderboard, which aimed to gather Codeforces-like data to automate kernel development, and also KernelBench.
insights.speaker: Alex Zhang (guest, MIT PhD)
insights.so_what: Kernel optimization is a natural RL domain with verifiable rewards, so it is ripe for automation.

insights.claim: The host cites a report that GPT 5.6 wrote more efficient kernels, making 'Terra and Luna' up to 80% cheaper to run, and notes that people without kernel experience have set records using auto-research loops.
insights.speaker: Host
insights.so_what: AI-written kernels translate directly into inference cost reductions.

insights.claim: Almost all recent GPU Mode leaderboard solutions are AI-generated. However, the only top-10 kernel that actually ran stably in real complex systems came from a veteran expert (Gorst) who used AI but steered it with his own hints, which highlights reward hacking and verification problems.
insights.speaker: Alex Zhang (guest, MIT PhD)
insights.so_what: Benchmarked AI kernel gains may overstate production value; verification is the bottleneck.

insights.claim: Zhang thinks the GPU kernel-writing field is almost oversaturated, since after FlashAttention and vLLM everyone started writing kernels.
insights.speaker: Alex Zhang (guest, MIT PhD)
insights.so_what: Marginal returns in standalone kernel work are falling; talent is moving up-stack.

insights.claim: Fused 'megakernels' are hard for LLMs because there is no training data for that class of problem. Since megakernels decompose into individual kernels, Zhang thinks a high-level compiler is better suited than LLM generation, and he notes a company working on this that has presented at GPU Mode.
insights.speaker: Alex Zhang (guest, MIT PhD)
insights.so_what: Compiler-based fusion companies have a defensible niche versus LLM kernel generation.

insights.claim: Kernel 'speed of light' is easy to compute for matmul but not for many tasks, and most hand-written kernels are not close to the theoretical limit. Optimizing kernels in isolation also misses cross-layer tradeoffs such as keeping data in cache for the next operation.
insights.speaker: Alex Zhang (guest, MIT PhD)
insights.so_what: Large end-to-end performance headroom remains at the whole-model level.

insights.claim: Deep domain expertise keeps its value even as AI produces kernels and mathematical proofs; labs still hire mathematicians for data labeling and for steering models.
insights.speaker: Alex Zhang (guest, MIT PhD)
insights.so_what: Expert-in-the-loop data and steering remain a durable labor market.

themes.theme: Beyond autoregressive decoders: neolab strategy and new model shapes

insights.claim: The 'Jev' model is interesting because it changes the language model's output space for very fast inference when there is task-specific prior knowledge. Asking a frontier LLM to do binary classification at roughly 400x the cost is 'ridiculous'.
insights.speaker: Alex Zhang (guest, MIT PhD)
insights.so_what: Specialized fast models built on LM backbones could take over high-volume, low-latency workloads.

insights.claim: Latency is the biggest bottleneck for RLMs and swarms. Trivial sub-calls could go to cheap, fast models, but today every call hits a bulky LLM, so new model types are needed.
insights.speaker: Alex Zhang (guest, MIT PhD)
insights.so_what: Demand for fast, small, specialized models rises as agentic systems scale.

insights.claim: Any lab other than OpenAI, Anthropic, possibly Meta, and Google DeepMind cannot win by copying the autoregressive-decoder recipe, because that competes on data and compute. Neolabs must bet on different paradigms, as Thinky does with interaction models.
insights.speaker: Alex Zhang (guest, MIT PhD)
insights.so_what: Evaluate neolabs on paradigm differentiation; me-too model labs are structurally disadvantaged.

insights.claim: Frontier labs have little incentive to spend large compute on new paradigm bets when the existing bet works, which creates room for neolabs.
insights.speaker: Alex Zhang (guest, MIT PhD)
insights.so_what: Innovator's dilemma at frontier labs supports funding of alternative-architecture startups.

insights.claim: The host argues that calibration is underrated: models return the most probable answer, not calibrated confidence. Synthetic data, generated against known ground truth, could train real calibration, which would enable cheap, trustworthy classifiers.
insights.speaker: Host
insights.so_what: Calibrated fast classifiers are an underexploited product opportunity.

insights.claim: The new fast model class targets latency-sensitive tasks like real-time games (such as Doom). Zhang's game benchmark for vision-language models shows that most models still cannot meaningfully beat these games, although Astra reportedly completed a Kirby game.
insights.speaker: Alex Zhang (guest, MIT PhD)
insights.so_what: Real-time agentic control remains an open capability frontier.

themes.theme: Research strategy, jagged intelligence and lab landscape

insights.claim: Academia's edge is big, risky bets on problems industry ignores. PhD students who chase benchmarks or whatever looks attractive to industrial labs waste that edge. SWE-bench was dismissed as an impossible task until Devin made its value obvious.
insights.speaker: Alex Zhang (guest, MIT PhD)
insights.so_what: Seminal ideas often look trivial or useless at first, so early-stage research signals deserve contrarian attention.

insights.claim: Zhang calls it absurd that a model as smart as Astra cannot reliably do simple work for a month the way an 18-year-old could. He considers this a solvable 'skills issue': with the right tooling, current models can do long, simple tasks consistently.
insights.speaker: Alex Zhang (guest, MIT PhD)
insights.so_what: Big near-term value is available from reliability tooling for long-horizon simple tasks, even without new models.
insights.quote: I believe It's absurd that we we can't do this make.

insights.claim: Jagged intelligence, with models disproportionately strong at code and math, implies those abilities could transfer to many domains through tools. Zhang poses the test of whether Astra, with all GPU-programming data removed, could learn kernel optimization in context, which frames the gap to humans as a tooling/continual-learning problem.
insights.speaker: Alex Zhang (guest, MIT PhD)
insights.so_what: Continual/in-context learning tooling is the bridge from code/math strength to broad economic tasks.

insights.claim: Zhang thinks Google DeepMind is somewhat overrated in agent systems. People he has talked to describe too much bureaucracy despite its talent and resources, and he doesn't know anyone who uses Antigravity. The host compares Google's phase to Meta's before it shipped products.
insights.speaker: Alex Zhang (guest, MIT PhD)
insights.so_what: Google's product execution remains the swing factor despite its research strength.

insights.claim: Sakana functions like a PhD-style research lab rather than an OpenAI/Anthropic competitor. It targets a different Japanese market with a culturally adapted Japanese model and chat product. Zhang adds that Chinese labs (such as Kimi's Delta attention work) have done very cool work.
insights.speaker: Alex Zhang (guest, MIT PhD)
insights.so_what: Regional and culturally specialized model companies can carve out non-frontier niches.

insights.claim: In open-ended research, the hardest problem is selecting the genuinely interesting outputs ('pearls') from a huge corpus of waste. Sakana's Fugu model router came out of the idea of picking the best solution for a task.
insights.speaker: Alex Zhang (guest, MIT PhD)
insights.so_what: Filtering and selection, not generation, is the bottleneck for autonomous research systems.

insights.claim: Speculative programmatic tool calling, which starts tool calls early by statically analyzing code the model is still writing, is a no-brainer for code-acting agents like RLM or CodeAct. It works much better in functional languages (Haskell, OCaml, Effect-TS) than in Python or JavaScript.
insights.speaker: Alex Zhang (guest, MIT PhD)
insights.so_what: A cheap latency win for agent frameworks, and a reason to favor typed/functional tool runtimes.

insights.claim: Human attention is now the scarce resource: Zhang struggles with the number of projects he runs and finds agents don't really help, since one tends to launch a prompt and never check on it.
insights.speaker: Alex Zhang (guest, MIT PhD)
insights.so_what: Agent-management and oversight tooling addresses a real pain point for heavy users.
